articles.title: What strike on Russian ship in Libya says about spread of Ukraine war
articles.summary: Ukraine's sinking of a Russian battleship at a port in Libya raises the stakes of the war a notch, writes Frank Gardner.
articles.body:
Anchored in a Mediterranean harbour nearly 2,000 miles from Moscow, the Captain of Russia's corvette Merkury might well have thought his ship was safe from attack. It wasn't.

The audacious and successful night-time attack in Benghazi , co-ordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and its armed forces, has raised the obvious question: is the Ukraine war spreading well beyond its borders?

The answer is yes, in fact, it was already spreading. But this attack, which Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky called "an exemplary operation" will inevitably raise the stakes another notch.

Russia, which is currently engaged in a non-stop campaign to batter Ukraine's civilian population into submission with daily missile and drone strikes , has called it "a dangerous escalation".

It follows the suspected Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian dry-cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland at the weekend, which the Kremlin described as an act of terrorism.

Ukraine's long-range drones have also previously struck Russia's Baltic oil terminal at Ust-Luga.

Some of Ukraine's more audacious long-range drone attacks – what Zelensky likes to call "long-range sanctions" – have also struck targets thousands of kilometres beyond Ukraine's borders with Russia, deep inside Siberia.

The most notable of these was last year's Operation Spider's Web, which involved a specially adapted lorry that drove close to a Russian strategic nuclear bomber airbase and released a "swarm" of explosive drones that damaged or destroyed several expensive bombers.

And Ukraine has also been active further south in Africa where its forces have targeted Russian mercenaries from the Africa Corps, the successor to the infamous Wagner Group that was accused of carrying out numerous human rights abuses.

It's not just Russia that will be alarmed by this latest Ukrainian operation in Benghazi harbour. The United Nations mission in Libya has already expressed its "deep concern".

Libyan officials point out that their country is not a party to the Russia-Ukraine war, although the Merkury and an accompanying cargo ship that was also hit were berthed in the eastern part of Libya controlled by the pro-Moscow warlord and self-styled "Field Marshal" Khalifa Haftar.

Throughout this year the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) has condemned all attacks on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and today the global shipping community will be wondering whether this attack does indeed set a dangerous precedent.

If Ukraine can plan and execute such a bold attack on Russian ships in a nominally neutral harbour so far from home, where does this stop?

As the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches, this war has already been spreading, notably in other parts of Europe.

On Friday, several Russian projectiles landed well inside Poland's borders , just 60 miles from an Anglo-French exercise of forces intended to be deployed following an eventual ceasefire in Ukraine.

This, said Poland's PM Donald Tusk, was "a deliberate provocation" by Moscow.

It's not the first time Russian munitions have landed inside Poland, and therefore inside Nato territory, but observers have pointed out that Russia's probing of Nato's borders is becoming ever more brazen and some are calling for a firmer response.

But Russia is already heavily sanctioned by the West, with Europe having reduced much – but not all – of its energy imports from Russia, so the options for retaliation are limited, short of military confrontation, which no one wants.

Both Romania and Moldova have found themselves frequently struck by overflying Russian drones targeting Ukraine's Black Sea ports, while Bulgaria and Romania have suffered maritime drone attacks on commercial shipping just offshore in the Black Sea.

In the case of Romania, a Nato member, fast jets have had to be scrambled to intercept incoming Russian drones and there is a profound suspicion that these incursions are not all accidental.

The three Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – all have borders with Russia and all consider themselves right on the front lines in this war.

There have been a number of anonymous attacks on military industrial facilities in these countries, blamed on agents acting on Moscow's behalf.

Russia, for its part, suspects Estonia of being complicit in Ukrainian drone attacks on the Baltic involving overflights through Estonian airspace.

Hybrid warfare isn't new but it is on the rise.

It refers to the practice, by either side, of carrying out largely anonymous and unattributable operations using methods like cyber attacks, the burning down of warehouses supplying military equipment and the dispatching of drones, both for surveillance and loaded with explosives.

This autumn, Germany's Leipzig-Halle airport, which is used as a resupply hub by Ukraine's cargo aircraft, was targeted by three explosive drones that were discovered before anyone was hurt.

There have been other incidents involving explosive packages sent across Europe targeting Germany, Poland and the UK. Moscow denies any involvement.

articles.title: California nursing student and mom arrested months after man’s body turns up in ravine: police
articles.summary: A truck driver's call near Livermore, California, led police to Marcelino Perez Jimenez's body in a ravine and a murder investigation reaching San Jose.
articles.body: A truck driver’s roadside stop near Livermore, California, led police to a man’s body in a ravine and, eventually, to a 22-year-old nursing student and her mother. The driver called 911 on Aug. 25 after spotting what appeared to be a body below the road, KTVU FOX 2 reported. Alameda County sheriff’s deputies found Marcelino Perez Jimenez who had been stabbed multiple times. San Jose police say they believe he was killed in an apartment where he was last seen three days earlier. HIKER IN GEORGIA MAKES DISTURBING DISCOVERY ON MOUNTAIN Jimenez had gone into the apartment with Alexia Nieves Solache on Aug. 22. She was carrying a 24-pack of beer, according to charging documents reviewed by The Mercury News. The next day, security cameras at the complex allegedly caught Solache and her mother, Veronica Rangel, struggling to move a heavy box. The women used a hand truck to get it into a rental car, the documents said. WIFE AND DAUGHTER ARRESTED AFTER DNA IDS MAN WHOSE SEVERED HEAD WAS FOUND IN TRASH BAG Police say investigators traced a vehicle from the complex to the stretch of road near the ravine where Jimenez was found. Police arrested Solache in Los Angeles on Oct. 27 and took Rangel, 55, into custody in San Jose the same day. Both were booked on suspicion of murder, police said. MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING PARTNER ARRESTED IN MEXICO NEARLY TWO YEARS AFTER FLEEING WITH THEIR TWO CHILDREN Solache faces a murder charge, and Rangel is accused of helping conceal the crime, The Mercury News reported. Rangel was released under supervision and told the outlet she believes her daughter acted in self-defense. How Solache and Jimenez knew each other remains unclear. articles.title: Search continues for Lindsey Doerr, last seen walking alone in Accident, Maryland, in 2023
articles.summary: Thirty-nine-year-old Lindsey Doerr was last seen on November 4, 2023, walking alone in a wooded area of Accident, Maryland, carrying golf clubs. Maryland State Police are investigating.
articles.body: Lindsey Doerr was on the road to recovery. In the fall of 2023, she was back home in Accident, Maryland, after a brief hospital stay. Lindsey’s family says she was settling in when she suddenly disappeared. Nicole Skidmore has known Lindsey for most of their lives. They went to the same middle and high schools in Garrett County. Although they weren’t particularly close, their paths crossed again as adults. “It’s a very rural community,” Nicole told Dateline. “And everybody’s kind of in everybody’s business.” After college, Nicole ended up working with Lindsey’s aunt, Marilyn Holliday. She says Marilyn would fill her in on what was going on in Lindsey’s life. According to Nicole, Lindsey had fallen into a rough crowd and reached out to her in the spring of 2023 for advice. “She was trying to turn her life around,” Nicole said. “It seemed like she was looking for a friend, um, someone that wasn’t in her circle.” But they never had the chance to fully reconnect. Marilyn Holliday is the family spokesperson. She told Dateline that in the fall of 2023, her niece was hospitalized for several days. She was released in the beginning of November and her mother, Robin, brought her home. “My sister has a small store in Addison,” Marilyn said. It’s a mom-and-pop market in rural Pennsylvania, near the Maryland border. Robin spends most of her time there but also owns a home on about 100 acres in a heavily-wooded area on Doerr Road in Accident. Lindsey was living in a trailer near that property. According to Marilyn, who lives nearby, Lindsey was settling back into her daily life. She is a type 1 diabetic and had plans to get more insulin at the pharmacy and to purchase a cellphone. Marilyn says her sister Robin went to Accident to check on Lindsey on November 10, 2023. The heat was off in the trailer and Lindsey was nowhere to be found. That night, Robin started messaging Lindsey’s friends to see if anyone knew where she was. No one did. The next day, Robin checked the trailer again, and Lindsey still wasn’t there. That’s when Marilyn was told Lindsey was missing. “Right away, I jumped in my car,” Marilyn said. “We were all hoping that Lindsey had just wandered off somewhere and that she would be found.” Nicole Skidmore learned Lindsey was missing on November 11, when she saw a post on Robin’s Facebook page that said Lindsey hadn’t been seen and asked if people could help search for her. Like Marilyn, she also jumped into action. “That first search day, I started searching the outskirts, the, um, areas that I had learned Lindsey frequented,” Nicole said. According to Marilyn, Lindsey had recently been exhibiting what she described as paranoid behavior. She believed “someone was after her” and that her phone and other people’s phones were bugged. Lindsey no longer had a phone at the time of her disappearance. Her wallet and insulin were found in the trailer. Maryland State Police McHenry Barrack took the missing persons report from Lindsey’s mom on November 11. “Robin advised she last saw Lindsey at her residence on Friday, November 3, in the evening,” Detective Sergeant Ted Bell told Dateline. During the initial search, a family member checked his hunting trail cameras. One of the cameras captured Lindsey at 8:57 a.m. on November 4. Maryland State Police confirmed it was the last known sighting of her. She was wearing a blue tank top, black pants, and was carrying golf clubs. Bell says Lindsey had been known to take golf clubs on her walks and hit balls in the woods. Maryland State Police conducted their first organized search for Lindsey on November 16. “We had people from all over the state come up,” Bell said. The search involved the aviation division, cadaver dogs, and the special operations division. Bell says Lindsey disappeared in a “heavily-wooded and very treacherous” area. “There’s steep ravines and creek bottoms,” he explained. During their first search, authorities found a coat belonging to Lindsey along the path between her trailer and the trail camera. The golf clubs were later discovered in a different location. “Those were on a neighboring property a good distance away from where the trail camera picture was or where the first couple searches were focused,” Bell noted. Nicole mapped out the locations where Lindsey was last seen and where her belongings were found. She says a shoe was also found that the family believes belonged to Lindsey, although investigators could not verify the shoe was hers. “The coat and the golf clubs are the only ones that they could definitively say were hers,” Bell said. Three years later, Lindsey remains missing. “Every indication we have and gut feeling is that she’s still out there in the -- in the woods there,” Bell said. “I drive past the property a lot with my job,” Nicole told Dateline. “Every time I drive by, I remember she’s gone.” Now, whenever she can, Nicole continues to look for her old friend. After three years, Marilyn realizes that the chances of finding Lindsey alive are slim. But the family is still hoping for answers. “I’m always hoping, like, during hunting season, that somebody will just happen to be out there in the woods and find something,” she said. Lindsey’s family is offering a $5,000 reward for her location. Lindsey is 5’2”, 120 lbs. She has blue eyes and strawberry-blonde hair. She was last seen wearing a blue tank top and black pants. She would be 42 years old today. Anyone with information regarding Lindsey’s disappearance is encouraged to contact the Maryland State Police McHenry Barrack at 301-387-1101. articles.title: A Sri Lankan man sought over £7 million from the UK Home Office for alleged detention injuries; surveillance footage showed him carrying out daily activities, and the High Court found his claim fundamentally dishonest
articles.summary: A Sri Lankan man who sought more than £7 million from the UK Home Office claimed that immigration detention had left him severely mentally ill and unable
articles.body: A Sri Lankan man who sought more than £7 million from the UK Home Office claimed that immigration detention had left him severely mentally ill and unable to speak, work or care for himself. Vengadeswara Raw Gopalakrishnan said his condition had caused lasting damage and made him dependent on others.However, the High Court found that he had deliberately fabricated or exaggerated his symptoms. According to the High Court judgment, Vengadeswara Raw Gopalakrishnan v The Home Office [2026] EWHC 2856 (KB), surveillance footage showed him carrying out everyday activities that contradicted his claims. The court also examined evidence about his family life and work before ruling that his personal injury claim was fundamentally dishonest. The judge found that the dishonesty had been present since the claim was introduced in 2014.How did an asylum challenge turn into a £7 million damages claimGopalakrishnan came to the UK in 2010 and overstayed after his student visa expired in 2012. He made an unsuccessful asylum application in August 2013 and was held in immigration detention from September 2013 until February 2014, when he was released on health grounds. His original legal challenge arose from his period of detention and was brought in October 2013 as an application for judicial review. It challenged the refusal of his asylum application and the decision to remove him to Sri Lanka. A personal injury claim was added in 2014, alleging that his treatment in detention had caused severe psychological harm.The case later included claims of false imprisonment over his detention and negligence concerning his treatment while in custody. He claimed that he had suffered pain, injuries, financial losses, and other damage as a result. In 2023, he was granted indefinite leave to remain, and the public law issues were settled. However, his personal injury claim continued in the High Court as a damages case. Since 2014, Gopalakrishnan had been described as lacking the capacity to conduct legal proceedings himself. His case was therefore handled by a litigation friend, Reena Mathew, who was said to know him through their local church and provide care for him voluntarily.What did surveillance footage reveal about his daily activitiesThe Home Office instructed enquiry agents to observe Gopalakrishnan between 12 May and 2 June 2026. The judge watched footage showing him taking children to school, driving with Mathew and three children, using a mobile phone and interacting with people at a trampoline venue and restaurant. He was also filmed walking alone in public, including to a pharmacy, and completing an hour-long gym session. Online searches showed him taking part in a go-karting competition on 19 April 2025. The Home Office also obtained Mathew’s file, which described Gopalakrishnan as her spouse and the father of their children. Birth certificates recorded him as the father of two children and listed his occupation as a delivery driver in both records, alongside other evidence.The couple's relationship and family life raised questions about earlier claimsMedical experts had been given accounts that Gopalakrishnan could barely communicate, needed extensive care and could not work. Mathew had presented herself as a volunteer. However, both later stated that they had first met in 2012, before his detention, and met again in 2014, when they began a relationship. They started living together in 2015 and have three children, born on 28 October 2019, 1 June 2021 and 19 August 2025.Mathew said she had not disclosed their relationship because she was not allowed another person living in her accommodation and feared it could affect her immigration status. The judge rejected her claim that she did not intend to mislead.The judge found that the earlier accounts concealed their domestic circumstances. He also noted that Gopalakrishnan had not provided a clear explanation of his recovery or his abilities when addressing the court.High Court found his £7 million personal injury claim fundamentally dishonestThe judge accepted evidence from the Home Office’s psychiatric expert, Professor Maden, who concluded that the symptoms had been fabricated or exaggerated. The court found that Gopalakrishnan had deliberately feigned an inability to communicate during expert assessments and had knowingly participated in false accounts given by Mathew. It ruled that the dishonesty went to the root of the personal injury claim, which sought damages for pain, lost earnings and lifelong care.The High Court found, on the balance of probabilities, that Gopalakrishnan had deliberately fabricated or grossly exaggerated his symptoms, working with Reena Mathew to pursue more than £7 million in damages. The judge ruled that the personal injury claim had been fundamentally dishonest from the time it was introduced in 2014, as the alleged injuries formed the basis of compensation claims, lost earnings and lifelong care. Gopalakrishnan had discontinued the claim after the Home Office presented new evidence.However, as Gopalakrishnan had discontinued his claim, the court ruled that he was liable to pay the Home Office's costs for the entire case up to the date the notice of discontinuance was served. The judge also granted the Home Office permission to enforce the costs order in full extent. The judge clarified that no findings were made on the merits of the separate false imprisonment or public law claims.Disclaimer: This article is based on the High Court judgment in Vengadeswara Raw Gopalakrishnan v The Home Office [2026] EWHC 2856 (KB), concerning claims arising from his immigration detention, the evidence presented during the proceedings, the court's finding of fundamental dishonesty in his personal injury claim and the resulting costs order. The Times of India has not independently verified the allegations, medical evidence or surveillance footage referred to in the judgment.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
articles.summary: The publisher of an essay on coercive control apologises for "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".
articles.body:
Gisèle Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms Gisèle Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line .

articles.title: A Michigan woman inherited her mother's home in 2013, but it sold at foreclosure for about $180,000 after a deed gave her six months to redeem instead of the 12 required by law; a November 20 appeal revived her claim
articles.summary: A foreclosure sale can put a family's home beyond reach, but what happens when the legal documents give the former owner less time to reclaim the property
articles.body: A foreclosure sale can put a family's home beyond reach, but what happens when the legal documents give the former owner less time to reclaim the property than the law actually allows? A Michigan woman who inherited her mother's house faced that situation after a sheriff's deed incorrectly stated that she had six months, rather than 12, to redeem the property following foreclosure.In a published opinion issued on November 20, 2026, available on Justia, the Michigan Court of Appeals revived part of Cynthia Zalewski's challenge to the foreclosure sale, ruling that the incorrect deadline was a significant irregularity in the process. However, the court did not overturn the foreclosure sale or establish that Zalewski was entitled to get her home back. It sent the case back to the lower court to determine whether the error actually prejudiced her ability to preserve the property.A home inherited from her motherThe dispute began with a mortgage taken out by Zalewski's mother, Dorothy, in 2007. The loan secured $50,000 in debt. Dorothy died in January 2013, leaving the property to her daughter, who began making the mortgage payments after inheriting the home. By the time Zalewski made her last payment to the mortgage servicer, NewRez LLC, the outstanding principal was approximately $5,800. She alleged that in 2021, after her income declined during the COVID-19 pandemic, she informed NewRez about her financial difficulties and was offered a payment moratorium. She made no further payments after that arrangement.The mortgage was subsequently assigned to US Bank, which became involved in the foreclosure process. Zalewski said she first realised there was a problem when she discovered a notice posted at the property announcing a sheriff's sale. On December 12, 2023, the house was sold at the sheriff's sale to HP Foreclosure Solution for approximately $180,000. The accompanying evidence of sale stated that the amount owed was $18,788.02 and gave Zalewski six months to redeem the property.Why the redemption period became a legal issueUnder Michigan law, a homeowner's redemption period can depend on the amount remaining on the mortgage. When the outstanding balance is less than two-thirds of the original indebtedness, the applicable period is 12 months. In Zalewski's case, the amount stated as owed was substantially below two-thirds of the original $50,000 loan. The parties did not dispute that she was legally entitled to 12 months, despite the sheriff's deed specifying only six.After the sale, Zalewski contacted representatives of HP, Genisys Credit Union and Donald White, an employee of the credit union, to explain that the deadline was incorrect. She also attempted to arrange a new loan through Genisys to redeem the property. However, a three-day cooling-off period meant the loan could not be processed before the stated six-month deadline expired. Zalewski subsequently filed a lawsuit on October 31, 2024, challenging the foreclosure and raising several claims against the parties involved.The lower court recognised that the correct redemption period was 12 months but dismissed her foreclosure-related claims, reasoning that she had failed to redeem the property within that period and therefore lacked standing to challenge the sale.Appeals court says the deed contained a significant irregularityThe Michigan Court of Appeals disagreed with the lower court's treatment of the incorrect deadline as merely a clerical or typographical mistake. The judges explained that a sheriff's deed is legally required to state when it becomes effective if the property is not redeemed. Giving a homeowner six months instead of the legally required 12 could influence how the former owner or a third party understood the deadline.The court therefore held that the incorrect redemption period constituted an irregularity in the foreclosure procedure. However, it emphasised that proving an irregularity alone was not enough to overturn a foreclosure sale. Zalewski would also have to establish that the mistake caused her prejudice and that she would have been in a better position to preserve her ownership interest if the error had not occurred. Because the lower court had not examined those questions, the appeals judges sent that part of the case back for further proceedings.The court also upheld the dismissal of Zalewski's fiduciary-duty claim against Genisys and White, finding that their relationship was an ordinary lender-borrower arrangement rather than a fiduciary one. The November 20 ruling reversed the lower court's decision in part concerning HP and US Bank, affirmed other parts of the judgment and remanded the case. It gives Zalewski another opportunity to pursue her foreclosure challenge, but whether she can ultimately have the sale set aside remains unresolved.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Family of nine-year-old King Sha'Mar Overton filed a $100 million wrongful-death lawsuit after he drowned at a Virginia summer camp, alleges the camp allowed him into a swimming pool despite knowing he couldn't swim
articles.summary: A summer programme meant to teach a nine-year-old boy how to swim has become the centre of a $100 million wrongful-death lawsuit after he drowned at a
articles.body: A summer programme meant to teach a nine-year-old boy how to swim has become the centre of a $100 million wrongful-death lawsuit after he drowned at a Virginia facility. His family alleges that the camp failed to protect him despite being informed that he could not swim.King Sha'Mar Overton died on June 15, his first day at SwimRVA, a summer camp programme in Henrico County near Richmond, Courthouse News Service reported. His mother, LaTaisha Johnson, had enrolled him because she wanted him to learn swimming before a planned trip to South Carolina. She said she had made the camp staff aware of his inability to swim, both in person and in writing.Johnson said she expected the facility to provide a safe environment for her son. When she dropped him off, a staff member reportedly reassured her that he was at the right place. However, the family alleges that the precautions needed to protect a child who could not swim were not followed.According to the allegations, Overton entered the pool during a free-swimming session without a swimming partner or someone directly supervising him. He was underwater for at least 10 minutes before another child noticed him. His family believes that inadequate supervision and problems with the pool's safety arrangements led to his death.Attorney Ben Crump filed the $100 million lawsuit on October 16 on behalf of Johnson and the boy's sister, Khalil Hart. The complaint names SwimRVA, its counsellors and lifeguards, accusing them of gross and willful negligence. Attorney Mark Krudys is representing the family.Questions over lifeguards and pool arrangementsOne of the main issues raised by the family concerns the number and positioning of lifeguards at the facility. Krudys said the pool was required to have at least two lifeguards on duty. However, according to him, only one was present when the child drowned.The lawyer further alleged that the lifeguard on duty was not looking towards the shallow end of the pool. He also questioned why the lifeguard chair assigned to that section had been left unattended.Krudys said the absence of someone at that position was not an isolated occurrence. He alleged that the chair had been left vacant on earlier occasions as well.The family has also drawn attention to a large inflatable play structure installed in the middle of the pool. Johnson believes it may have restricted the lifeguard's view of the shallow end, making it difficult to notice a child in trouble.Accounts from people belonging to another group using the pool have added to the family's concerns. These witnesses reportedly said they saw several camp employees talking to one another rather than watching the swimmers shortly before the drowning.The family argues that the combination of inadequate supervision and the obstruction inside the pool raises questions about how the facility monitored children during swimming activities.Rescue attempts failed to revive the boyThe circumstances surrounding the rescue have also been described by the family's legal team. Overton was eventually brought out of the water by a person who was not employed by SwimRVA. An off-duty nurse who happened to be at the pool then attempted to revive him.The nurse performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) for around 10 minutes. Despite the efforts, the child could not be saved.Krudys described the condition in which Overton was found after being pulled out of the pool. He said water and foam came out of the boy's mouth, indicating how badly his lungs had been affected.The lawyer also referred to the nurse's account of the rescue attempt. According to him, she struggled to get oxygen into the child's lungs because they were filled with water.Another account from the pool concerned an alleged conversation between two employees during the emergency. A teacher associated with a different group at the facility said a man who appeared to be a SwimRVA manager asked another employee whether a swimming competition would have to be cancelled.This reportedly happened while paramedics were attending to Overton inside an ambulance nearby. The family has raised the incident as another concern about how the facility responded to the emergency.State licensing becomes another issue in the caseThe family has also questioned whether SwimRVA was operating under the required state licence when Overton drowned.Johnson said she learnt after her son's death that the programme had been running without a state licence. She believes this meant that state inspectors had not visited the facility to examine its operations.Krudys argued that a licensing inspection could have identified potential safety concerns at the swimming pool, including the placement of the large inflatable structure.The Virginia Department of Education said SwimRVA was operating in a capacity that required a licence. The facility subsequently changed its operating hours to avoid the licensing process.The licensing issue has become an important part of the family's allegations because it raises questions about the oversight of the programme. The family believes that an inspection could have brought attention to the pool's arrangements before the drowning took place.SwimRVA continued operating for the remainder of the summer after Overton's death. A separate incident occurred less than a month later when a poolhouse at the same location caught fire. Fire officials described that incident as accidental.Family seeks accountability through lawsuitThe family's legal action also follows concerns about the response from the camp and its employees after the incident.Krudys alleged that SwimRVA and its staff had not cooperated with the Henrico Commonwealth's Attorney's Office. He also said the facility's representatives had not spoken to Overton's family.Crump said the circumstances of the child's death prompted him to take up the case. He believes the lawsuit could help prevent similar incidents involving children at swimming programmes.At a press conference outside the Richmond courthouse, he questioned how a child could drown at a facility offering swimming lessons while instructors and other staff members were present.The family's complaint seeks $100 million in damages and accuses the camp and its employees of negligence. Krudys said the family would continue pursuing accountability even if prosecutors did not take action.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Michigan grandmother gave three grandchildren equal shares in family property in 1992; after one branch locked a gate in 2003, judges ruled the others waited too long to reclaim their stake
articles.summary: A Michigan couple who tried to reclaim their rights over jointly owned family land nearly 21 years after losing access to it have failed in their legal
articles.body: A Michigan couple who tried to reclaim their rights over jointly owned family land nearly 21 years after losing access to it have failed in their legal battle. An appeals court has ruled that they missed the deadline to challenge the loss of access, as the dispute had started much earlier than their lawsuit.According to the information available on Justia, the case centred on a property that had been shared by members of the Bullard family for decades. Its ownership began with a transfer in 1992, when Anna S. Bullard gave equal shares of the land to her three grandchildren, Jocelyn Bullard, Geoffrey Bullard and their sister Anna. Each received a one-third interest, allowing all three to hold ownership rights over the same property.Seven years later, the siblings decided to change the ownership arrangement. Geoffrey and Jocelyn agreed to buy their sister Anna's share for $400,000. Their spouses, Maria and Gerrit, were also part of the arrangement. The two siblings each borrowed $200,000 to meet their respective contributions towards the purchase.The family continued to share the property, but the arrangement ran into trouble in 2003. Jocelyn and Gerrit failed to repay the loan they had taken, which was secured against their interest in the land. To prevent the property from being taken over through foreclosure, Geoffrey and Maria stepped in and assumed responsibility for the debt. Jocelyn's mortgage was then cleared.The financial arrangement, however, changed how the family dealt with the property. Jocelyn and Gerrit became less involved in its management and finances. Jocelyn maintained that there was an understanding that Geoffrey would handle the rental income and use it to repay the amount they had contributed towards the mortgage. She said he did not agree to put this arrangement in writing.The disagreement also affected their ability to visit the land. Jocelyn said she made several attempts to enter the property from 2003 onwards but found the entrance gate locked. She also complained that Geoffrey did not give her access to the property's financial records. What followed was a lengthy dispute over whether the couple still had the right to use the land and whether they had waited too long to enforce that right.Couple approach court after years of disputeJocelyn and Gerrit eventually filed a lawsuit on May 29, 2024. They wanted the court to settle the ownership dispute and consider dividing the property between the parties. They alleged that Geoffrey and Maria had prevented them from entering the land and had withheld information about its finances.Geoffrey and Maria presented a different account. They maintained that they had been exercising control over the property as its sole owners since 2003. Their legal response included a claim based on adverse possession, a principle under which long-term possession of land can lead to ownership rights if certain legal conditions are met.They also argued that the couple had crossed the deadline for bringing a case over possession of the property. Michigan law generally allows 15 years for such claims.The trial court accepted their argument. It considered the locked entrance and the refusal to provide financial records as evidence that Geoffrey and Maria had taken control of the property to the exclusion of the other couple. It placed the beginning of that exclusion in 2003.This meant Jocelyn and Gerrit had until 2018 to seek legal relief. Since they approached the court only in 2024, the trial court dismissed their claims. The couple then challenged the decision before the Michigan Court of Appeals.Locked gate became crucial evidenceThe court examined the legal requirements for adverse possession. A person claiming ownership through this route must establish that their control of the land was visible, continuous and exclusive for the required period. The possession must also be without the owner's permission and must conflict with that owner's rights.However, the rules become more complicated when the people involved already own the property together. One co-owner's use of shared land does not automatically mean that the others have lost their rights. The law generally assumes that a person occupying jointly owned property continues to recognise the interests of the other owners.For that reason, the court said there must be clear evidence that one co-owner has attempted to keep another out. The excluded person must also have sufficient notice that their right to occupy the property is being challenged.Jocelyn and Gerrit argued that the circumstances did not establish such exclusion. They also referred to emails exchanged in 2016 and 2018, in which Geoffrey expressed interest in buying their share. According to the couple, these discussions showed that he continued to recognise their ownership.The appeals court did not accept this argument. It distinguished between recognising someone's ownership interest and allowing that person to exercise their rights over the property. The judges found that the discussions about a possible purchase did not undo the earlier actions that had prevented the couple from entering the land.Jocelyn's account of repeatedly finding the gate locked was particularly important. The court considered this direct evidence that she could not access the property. It also rejected the argument that the couple had to show that they specifically requested entry and were then refused.The judges concluded that the exclusion had become clear when Jocelyn encountered the locked gate in 2003. That was when the period for taking legal action began.2024 lawsuit falls outside legal deadlineThe appeals court calculated that the couple had 15 years from 2003 to bring their claim. Their deadline therefore ended in 2018, six years before they filed the lawsuit.The judges also considered the couple's objections to the trial court's assessment of the case but found no reason to overturn its decision.The ruling leaves the lower court's decision intact and rejects Jocelyn and Gerrit's attempt to reopen the dispute over their access to the family property.You use AI every day. articles.title: India, Nepal usher in 'golden chapter' in ties, Modi announces $ 1.63 billion package
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: India and Nepal looked to usher in a new chapter in ties, setting aside recent friction, as PM Narendra Modi announced a $ 1.63 billion (INR
articles.body: NEW DELHI: India and Nepal looked to usher in a new chapter in ties, setting aside recent friction, as PM Narendra Modi announced a $ 1.63 billion (INR 15,000 crore) largest ever economic package for the Himalayan nation after a meeting with counterpart Balendra Shah. The Nepal PM responded by declaring that India-Nepal ties stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as the ocean.India and Nepal also signed 8 MoUs as the leaders laid foundation stones for multiple cross-border infrastructure and energy initiatives, while virtually flagging off the Saryu-Kamala Express, a new rail service connecting Ayodhya to Janakpur in Nepal to boost religious tourism and people-to-people exchanges.A 10-point joint vision document, which will shape the roadmap for cooperation across various sectors, emphasised updating the bilateral legal framework - including through a review of the 1950 Treaty of Peace and Friendship - to ensure a forward-looking relationship. Both sides reaffirmed their commitment in the document to resolving all outstanding matters, including boundary disputes, through "constructive dialogue"."The bond between India and Nepal is not merely one of neighborhood, but of belonging and unshakeable trust. Our joys are shared, and so are our challenges. We are partners in each other’s progress, and a pillar of support for one another in difficult times," said Modi after what was his first meeting in person with Shah.In his remarks, Modi leveraged deep religious and spiritual links as an anchor for bilateral ties, referencing Ram, Sita and the Buddha and saying India and Nepal had the blessings of all 3. He said India and Nepal will also work together to enhance connectivity between Buddhist and Shiv-Shakti sacred sites in both countries, including Lumbini and Bodh Gaya.Expressing condolences for the loss of life caused by the devastating floods in Nepal in August, Modi said India's development cooperation package worth 24,000 crore Nepalese rupees ($1.63 billion) will give fresh momentum to Nepal’s reconstruction and long-term development. The package includes Rs 3500 crore as grant and remaining in the form of line of credit for energy projects.Modi called the joint vision document a blueprint to collectively realise their respective resolutions of a Viksit Bharat and Samunnat Nepal (Developed India and Prosperous Nepal). He said that together they were going to write a golden chapter in India-Nepal ties. The contentious boundary matter was also discussed in the meeting with the leaders directing the foreign secretaries to work on the outstanding related issues.Shah, who invited Modi to visit Nepal, said the leaders held candid, substantive, and forward-looking discussions and that "mutual respect, steadfast trust, and unbroken goodwill" are the bedrock of Nepal-India relations. The Nepal PM called for expanding air connectivity between the countries and the leaders agreed to convert the Kathmandu-Bhairahawa-Lucknow air route into a two-way route, allowing planes to fly back and forth along the same path instead of just one direction.The talks saw focus on border infrastructure as the leaders inaugurated the Dharchula road bridge connecting Uttarakhand and Nepal, and laid the foundation stone for the Banbasa Integrated Check Post (ICP). Modi said India remained committed to accelerating road and rail links via Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, while providing Nepal access to India’s Kandla and Paradip ports to facilitate smooth transit trade.Energy cooperation too figured prominently in the meeting with the leaders laying the foundation stone for the Lower Arun Hydroelectric Project and reiterating the commitment to timely completion of the Arun-3 project. They also inaugurated Motihari–Amlekhgunj Pipeline phase 2 and laid the foundation stone for the new Jhapa Petroleum Terminal, expanding fuel supply security for Nepal."For many years, India has been a reliable supplier of petroleum products and other essential commodities for Nepal. In keeping with the spirit of our Neighbourhood First Policy, despite serious challenges related to oil supply this year, we maintained the supply of fuel, fertilizers, and other essential items to Nepal," said Modi.The PM said Nepal’s rivers hold immense potential for clean energy and India’s vast energy market can turn this potential into a strong foundation for Nepal’s economic prosperity.In his remarks, Shah stressed the "incomparable bond" shared by the people of India Nepal. "The ties between Nepal and India stand as firm as the Himalayas and as vast as the ocean, a closeness so profound that words alone can scarcely capture it. As a dependable and trusted neighbor, India has consistently stood as a first responder in times of natural disasters and difficult hours," he said.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: EU plans sports ban in sweeping new Russia sanctions proposal
articles.summary: Proposed sanctions aim to curb Russian crypto financing and ‘propaganda’ in sports.
articles.body:
The European Commission has proposed new sanctions against Russia targeting its banks, crypto platforms, and participation in sporting events.

Commission chief Ursula von der Leyen introduced the 22nd package of sanctions on Monday, which includes a ban on Russian teams and individual athletes competing under the country’s flag at events in the European Union.

“We are striking harder at Russia’s ways to finance its war, by targeting its banks and crypto platforms,” von der Leyen wrote in a post on X, adding that the EU will be “shutting the door to its participation in European sports and cultural events”.

Von der Leyen said 60 banks will be removed from the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) messaging system used for international payments under the new proposals, which are intended to maintain economic pressure on Russia, almost five years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

She announced the creation of a crypto sanctions task force seeking to curb countries helping Russia to evade sanctions.

The commission also proposed a ban on visas for Russians who had fought in the war in Ukraine.

“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said.

The plan also put forward restrictions on financial flows from Russian sponsors to sports and cultural associations based in the EU. Russian nationals would also no longer be allowed to hold leadership positions on the governing bodies of sports federations.

“Sports events cannot be a forum for propaganda activities,” said von der Leyen.

The proposed package must be endorsed by all 27 EU member countries before going into force and comes just over a month after the bloc posted the largest listing of sanctions against Russia, targeting about 1,600 Russian officials and companies linked to its arms industry.

The EU has already slapped sanctions on more than 4,200 people and entities, including Russian President Vladimir Putin and several energy companies.

articles.title: NATO warns Putin could strike before European army responds, points to US as military model
articles.summary: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Russia's war machine runs at full speed and could threaten Europe long after the war in Ukraine ends.
articles.body: NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte warned Monday that creating a separate European army could undermine the alliance’s ability to respond quickly to a Russian attack, as Moscow continues to ramp up its military capabilities during the ongoing war in Ukraine. Speaking at the 72nd annual session of the NATO Parliamentary Assembly in Berlin, Rutte cautioned that competing military command structures could hold up decisions in a crisis, warning that Russia’s "war machine" is running at full throttle and could also pose a threat to Europe long after the war ends. "What I would counsel against is having all the nations with their own militaries working together in NATO and then on top of that having a big European structure, because then if Putin attacks, we will first need two or three weeks to agree who will do what, and then he will probably end up in Rotterdam before we have decided. So that has been my argument," Rutte said, according to Ukrainska Pravda. NATO JETS SHOOT DOWN DRONE IN LITHUANIAN AIRSPACE AS RUSSIA GROWS 'INCREASINGLY RECKLESS,' RUTTE SAYS Rutte pointed to the United States as a model for an integrated military, arguing that European countries would also need to move beyond separate national forces to establish a unified army. "My point has always been that if you have a European military, you cannot also have national militaries. The United States has one military." "There is not a specific army or navy for the state of New York or for the state of California. It is an integrated United States military. If Europe is able to pull that off, fine," Rutte said. Rutte said it was Russia's expanding military production and cooperation with China, Iran and North Korea that pose a long-term threat to NATO, regardless of how the war in Ukraine ends. "We face great dangers coming from Russia and the fact that Russia works so closely together with Iran, China, and North Korea, we know that Russia's war machine at the moment is running at full speed," Rutte also said at the assembly in Berlin. FOREIGN LEADER ON PUTIN’S DOORSTEP SOUNDS ALARM OVER IRAN FUELING MOSCOW’S WAR MACHINE "Its war economy keeps growing, and it won't stand still when the war against Ukraine hopefully will end one day. That whole machine is there and will continue." Rutte also rejected the idea that only countries bordering Russia or Ukraine face a direct military threat, warning that Moscow's long-range missiles put capitals across Europe within striking distance. "Let me say once again to everyone here who is not on the eastern flank: I have news for you. You are on the eastern flank too. These latest Russian missiles need only five minutes longer to reach Lisbon, Rome or The Hague, my hometown, than to reach Tallinn, Warsaw or Helsinki," Rutte said. "So we are all on the eastern flank here. Let's put an end to this discussion about whether or not you are on the eastern flank. We are all on the eastern flank." The NATO chief's remarks came amid plans to deploy an early-warning aircraft to Poland after Polish prosecutors said three Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles landed on Polish territory Friday during strikes against Ukraine. NATO WARNS RUSSIA: 'WE WILL BREAK' FORCES, DESTROY 'ANYTHING AND EVERYTHING' IF YOU ATTACK Polish Deputy Defense Minister Pawel Zalewski said that NATO would deploy an Airborne Warning and Control System, or AWACS, aircraft to strengthen surveillance along the alliance's eastern flank, according to Reuters. "This is a very good system that gives us even deeper... operational awareness which allows us to respond better to this kind of threat," Zalewski told reporters following a NATO meeting in Brussels. The aircraft can monitor large areas of airspace and provide allied forces with a shared picture of potential aerial threats, improving NATO's ability to detect and respond to missile and aircraft activity. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy also warned Monday night that intelligence indicated Moscow was preparing a new wave of strikes against Ukraine. Beyond Russia's ongoing military threats, Rutte said that Europe's interconnected infrastructure, including energy networks and communications systems, is vulnerable. RUSSIA'S SHADOW WAR IS PUTTING EUROPE ON EDGE AS GERMANY CONFRONTS A GROWING THREAT "We are all targeted, that we are all affected when it comes to our pipelines, our cables, our energy grids, and our economies." "They are all interconnected, and that means that we are all in this for the long term. And therefore, we must step up to the plate to ensure that we stay ahead of danger." Rutte said defending NATO countries demands civilian preparedness, pointing to northern European nations that have begun teaching residents about their responsibilities in the event of war. "This really takes the whole of society," he said. "And that's in the end, I think, still Norway and Sweden, and Denmark and Finland, and maybe one or two others who are really ahead of the pack here, and having made clear to their citizens what they need to do in case war breaks out, at least not to get in the way of the military, but to be helpful and also how they make sure that the police and the ambulance services and fire, the fire fighting departments work together, supporting the military wherever possible." Rutte's warnings come amid uncertainty over Ukraine's long-term security arrangements and whether Western allies will offer guarantees resembling NATO's Article 5 collective defense commitment as part of a future peace agreement. articles.title: Why I don't always tell potential employers I'm dyslexic
articles.summary: Many dyslexic people say it harms their confidence, a report about experiences in the workplace suggests.
articles.body:
Nineteen-year-old Ayana Bailey doesn't always disclose her dyslexia in job applications, in case it counts against her.

"It's not like there's going to be a target on my back, but I'm just like, 'maybe they won't select me'," says Bailey, a part-time florist.

A British Dyslexia Association (BDA) survey of more than 1,200 working dyslexic adults found Bailey isn't alone - with 46% hiding their dyslexia at work.

Some 81% believe the condition adds to their work-related stress.

Bailey was diagnosed aged 11 and says she received good support at school, including mentoring, which helped her to understand her strengths and manage low self-esteem.

But the world of work has proved more challenging.

For Bailey, the application process is "daunting". She says she relies on her mum to go through it with her.

In interviews, Bailey says: "I just shut down. I completely forget who I am."

One way of coping, she says, is to have a little script, but she admits it doesn't always work.

Bailey, who studied film and wants to go into the creative arts, says that while dyslexia has sometimes made her feel anxious, it's also given her opportunities.

"I would definitely say my creativity and thinking outside the box [is my biggest strength]."

She says her dyslexia makes her a visual learner - able to imagine characters before seeing any written descriptions and helping her dream of becoming a casting director.

For nurse Lisa Daniels, her dyslexia meant leaving work more than an hour late most days just to finish the paperwork.

"I suppressed it. I was like 'Oh no, everything is fine. It's not affecting me.'" In reality, she says "it was majorly affecting me".

Daniels, 37, says a previous manager was dismissive of her request for adjustments.

"When I first started, they said, 'Oh they are babying some of these nurses' and I didn't have the confidence to challenge it."

She says her suggestions of having more accessible fonts and colours on documents were not listened to.

Five years into her career, Daniels' colleague told her about a staff network on neurodiversity and her confidence grew, along with adjustments such as noise-cancelling headphones.

"I have that resilience that, despite the sometimes lack of support, I'm still gonna show up. I'm still gonna try."

Daniels says she's now recovered from her imposter syndrome.

Over half of people surveyed by the BDA say dyslexia makes them feel bad about themselves, while 39% have experienced bad mental health related to it.

The BDA is calling for workplaces to make reasonable adjustments for employees who need them, even without a diagnosis, and wants managers to be trained to understand and support dyslexic employees.

Its report finds dyslexic employees often have to put extra effort into work, finding their own ways to cope if systems, processes and communication are not accessible.

There are 3.3 million dyslexic adults currently in employment, estimates the BDA. Some told the report:

"I have to cope with little comments that are seen as banter about my spelling."

"My line manager is actually dyslexic and we happily talk about it. We share best practice and war stories."

"It would be nice to be seen as intellectual. Just because I cannot always write as well as others, doesn't mean I don't have the knowledge."

"I revealed my dyslexia quite early on in my employment… I do believe it was used as a stick to beat me with."

"I feel like I have got to do more, be more, show more... because I've got this deficit of being dyslexic".

Employment law solicitor Jenna Ide helped a client win a high-profile dyslexia discrimination case against Starbucks in 2016.

"Many dyslexic employees start a new job already struggling with low self-esteem," she says.

"That's especially true of dyslexics who are late-diagnosed and who may have spent years at school and in earlier jobs believing they just weren't clever enough.

"When an employer doesn't understand dyslexia, relies on inaccessible ways of working and doesn't offer support, it reinforces those feelings and can make people more reluctant to ask for help."

Kate Griggs, founder of UK charity Made By Dyslexia, agrees recruitment can still be a barrier, particularly when it is skewed toward written applications and timed tests.

"My advice to young dyslexics is simple: know your strengths, own them and talk about them with confidence. Ask for the support you need and different ways to show what you can do. Find the roles where those strengths are valued."

Ellen Broomé, head of the British Dyslexia Association, said: "Dyslexic people should not have to work harder simply to have the same opportunities as their colleagues.

"Our research reveals the hidden cost many pay, spending additional time and energy compensating for workplaces that fail to understand or support them.

"This is not a question of ability, ambition or talent. It is about the barriers people face and the opportunities lost when workplaces fail to recognise and support different ways of thinking and working."

articles.title: I pay £250 a month for someone else to do my life admin - it's worth it
articles.summary: Busy mothers on both sides of the Atlantic are paying companies to handle their to-do lists.
articles.body:
Maxine Dillion, a busy 44-year-old mum of two, was struggling with her life admin – the never-ending to-do list of household and personal chores.

Everything from arranging for a handyman to fix something, to posting her clothing returns on Vinted, she wasn't getting around to it.

"I felt like all the little jobs that I didn't have time for were mounting up," says Maxine, who is self-employed helping businesses with their use of social media.

Then last year, Maxine, who lives in Mansfield in Nottinghamshire, discovered a new company called Life Laundry.

Launched in 2025 by two women based in Wakefield, Yorkshire, you can pay them to do all your admin jobs for you. Such companies are known as life personal assistants, and in recent years a growing number have sprung up on both sides of the Atlantic.

Maxine, who earns £32,000 a year, doesn't have a massive amount of disposable income, but she decided to start spending £250 a month for five hours' work and thinks it is worth it as it also helps reduce her "mental load" .

The owners of Life Laundry, Alicia Papachristou and Jane Forbes, now look after a host of things for Maxine. Other jobs they take care of include arranging insurance, sending school emails, and managing online subscriptions.

Much of the work they can do remotely, but once a month they travel to Mansfield to do the jobs that require them to be physically present.

"If someone asks us what we do, we say we're life PAs [personal assistants], and we ease your overwhelm," says Forbes.

With such companies also increasingly available in the US, another busy working mother, Amanda Sims Nichols in Austin, Texas, has also employed a firm to look after her life admin.

Amanda, who is a business consultant, has three children with her attorney husband, and decided to start paying for help with life admin after moving house, away from her family support network.

She pays $2,250 (£1,750) a month for 25 hours, and says she relishes offloading regular chores including the weekly food shop and clothes washing.

"Money cannot buy you everything, but it can buy you back some of your time," says the 45-year-old.

The company she uses, Queen of To Do, was founded by Kate Ginsberg in 2011. She says that interest has greatly increased since the pandemic.

The business now has more than 50 active users. Meanwhile, Life Laundry has 25 customers.

Both companies say demand is growing for their services as people's lives become increasingly frantic.

Ginsberg says that the work they do for clients can be very diverse, with no task too big or too small.

Some of the larger tasks her team has faced over the years include flying from Austin to New York City to buy a desperately needed Christmas gift, and finding a new wedding location for a client with just three days' notice due to an incoming hurricane.

Jess Baker, a UK chartered psychologist, says the appeal of such providers is understandable.

"Using a life PA, if you can afford one, takes the pressure off having to keep hundreds of to-dos swimming around your head, or on lists you might forget to look at," she says.

"Otherwise, the cognitive load can lead to feelings of being overwhelmed, excess worry and exhaustion."

While paying for help with such tasks may seem a luxury, for some people support with life's everyday trials is a lifeline.

Anna Allington sought help after her husband died. "My husband passed away. I was 47," she says.

"And the same week he passed away, I got leukaemia. There was a lot to sort out and I was very, very unwell."

Anna, now 51, still suffers the after-effects of her cancer. "I can't function executively like I used to," she says.

She pays £1,200 a month for 40 hours of help from Cheshire-based company Vi-Va. Her personal assistant helps her respond to emails, manage her diary and make travel plans and bookings.

"We meet twice a week on Zoom," says Anna, who lives in the Cotswolds, so they can go through all her tasks.

Many more women than men use these companies.

Queen of To Do says just 20% of its clients are male, while only one of Life Laundry's 25 clients is a man.

Some of that disparity is likely due to mothers still looking after the lion's share of household admin, as studies continue to show.

However, Life Laundry's Forbes wonders if some men are too proud to ask for assistance.

"Men are struggling as well, but I think they're less likely to ask for help."

articles.title: South Africa femicide: Night-time curfews and street patrols after women murdered in Ekurhuleni
articles.summary: South African communities tell the BBC of measures they're taking to keep women safe after a wave of horrific killings.
articles.body:
Tuku Nkosiyaphantsi found out his daughter had been killed from a post on Facebook.

It was August and he hadn't been able to reach 27-year-old Okuhle for days, although it wasn't unusual for her to drop out of contact from time to time.

Then one Saturday, two of Tuku's neighbours called him to say that they had seen that Okuhle had been reported missing by police on Facebook. They had also seen a photo of what appeared to be Okuhle injured.

"When I looked at this photo, I saw that the person in it was dead, and when I looked closer I realised it was Okuhle," says Tuku, 50.

After seeing the image, Tuku phoned a police officer he knew. The policeman confirmed the woman in the picture had been killed and her body dumped near a river in Kokstad, an agricultural hub in South Africa's KwaZulu-Natal province, in the east of the country.

But because the morgue was closed for the weekend, it wasn't until Monday morning that Tuku was able to identify Okuhle's body.

When he did, Tuku saw she had been mutilated and her face badly beaten.

"It was very painful, so much that I cannot accept it."

Okuhle had two children, aged nine and three, and was a civil engineering student.

She is among 581 women who were killed in the country between July and September , according to the South African Police Service.

Overall, there were 5,590 murders - 204 fewer than in the same period last year.

It is the first time police have broken down murders by gender, so it is unclear whether the number of women killed is an increase or decrease on previous years.

There has been a renewed national outcry this year about the scale of violence against women after the partially naked and bruised bodies of 12 women were found dumped in public areas in Ekurhuleni, a district to the east of Johannesburg, this summer.

South Africa has one of the highest rates of gender-based violence and femicide - the intentional killing of a woman or girl - in the world.

In response to this summer's killings, President Cyril Ramaphosa promised safety audits across every municipality to identify and address dangerous spaces for women, as well as an increased police presence in the worst-affected areas.

But in places like Kokstad and Kempton Park, both in Ekurhuleni, the BBC World Service saw people taking the protection of women into their own hands.

For Tuku, that means investigating his daughter's killing himself.

Months after she was killed, he says no-one has been arrested.

"It was just silent after we buried Okuhle - there was nothing at all. I so wish the police would stand up and investigate."

He believes police failed to review CCTV footage from a local government building in the town that may have shown who his daughter was with on the day she disappeared. The footage is wiped every seven days, he says.

The BBC approached the South African Police Service for comment but at the time of publication, no response had been received.

The police service has previously acknowledged shortcomings in its overall response to gender-based violence and femicide, adding that it was continuing to invest in addressing these challenges. Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia has said there needs to be "greater efforts" to prevent violence against women and children.

According to a 2024 report by the South African Medical Research Council, the number of unsolved cases of femicide was growing.

This year, Amnesty International said South Africa's police service was "under-resourced, poorly equipped, and insufficiently trained to respond effectively and sensitively to gender-based violence".

Tuku says he is now searching for CCTV footage and seeking out people who knew his daughter in the hope of finding leads.

Despite Ramaphosa's promises, he has little faith anything will change.

"I listened to Ramaphosa. The government acts only when something happened. We in Kokstad, we feel like we are ignored and unseen. The government does not care for us."

Asked earlier this month by the BBC what progress South Africa had made to keep women safe, Ramaphosa said the government would be allocating extra money in February's budget to deal with gender-based violence.

Speaking as he cast his vote in local elections, Ramaphosa added that the government had increased police numbers in the last three years "and we will continue to do so, so that there can be more visible policing".

Okuhle is not the only woman to be killed this year in Kokstad.

Between January and October this year, the bodies of five women and three very young children were found in the town, with arrests only taking place in two of the cases.

In response, this summer, the community set up street patrols and a curfew for women and children.

Since June, children have been told to be indoors by sunset and women by 21:00.

Kamvalethu Cetywayo, 34, from a local neighbourhood watch group, leads a group of around 15 men who patrol crime hotspots in the town at night, including areas where bodies have been found or trouble has been reported to them.

The patrols tend to take place between Thursday and Sunday because this is when people drink alcohol most heavily, says Kamvalethu.

Most of the patrollers carry sticks, whips and torches, but Kamvalethu has a licensed gun. He says the group will call police when they need back-up.

Asked how he feels about restricting the freedoms of women and children, Kamvalethu says the curfew helps keep them safe, is voluntary, and a temporary measure until police arrest the killers.

"With the resolution we made with the community, we get to assist them with this, but if people are refusing there's nothing we can do."

Even so, not all victims are attacked at night or on the streets.

Kgothatso Mojela was kidnapped on her way to work in 2018 in Kempton Park.

She was in a taxi when the driver locked the doors and started driving in the wrong direction.

When Kgothatso told him he had missed the turn, she says he started punching and slapping her.

"Immediately, I just knew my life was in danger," says Kgothatso, who is now 35.

Kgothatso says she forced the passenger door open and threw herself out of the moving taxi, badly injuring her knee and causing nerve damage to her eyes. Two security guards, who were nearby, came to her aid.

She says her attacker was later jailed for a number of crimes, including what he did to her, but was released last year. Kgothatso says she now fears for her life.

Yet while Kgothatso was attacked by a stranger, according to the South African Medical Research Council, 60% of women murdered in the country between 2020-21 were killed by an intimate partner.

In the wake of her attack, Kgothatso has made changes to how she lives, including buying an imitation gun to scare off would-be attackers.

She has also stopped running alone, and insists on someone accompanying her if she goes to meet a client she hasn't met before at work.

Such precautions are all too familiar to many women in South Africa.

In September police urged women in the Kempton Park area to avoid walking or running alone, "particularly in isolated areas" - after the killing of 38-year-old mother Elizabeth Moselakgomo.

She vanished on 9 September while out running. Her badly bruised, partially clothed body was found dumped near a busy motorway in Kempton Park three days later .

It was a killing that resonated deeply within South Africa's running community, including sisters Zonke and Zama Mthethwa. They started The Pack, a women's running group in Johannesburg nine years ago. Elizabeth would sometimes attend The Pack events.

Grim discoveries of murdered women spark fear in South Africa

The South African men trying to end violence against women: 'Every man needs to play a part'

Runners across the city joined the search efforts following Elizabeth's disappearance, and took part in protests calling for violence against women to end.

Zonke and Zama's group now takes extra precautions during their runs, including carrying pepper spray and whistles. They also get cars to follow them and have started offering self-defence coaching to the women in their running group.

"We need to try and rally and create safe spaces for women to show up authentically and to do what they love doing," says Zama, 37.

Following her ordeal, Kgothatso moved from Kempton Park and now lives closer to her parents in another part of the country.

Her mother, a community activist, recently organised a prayer march to remember women who have been killed.

Kgothatso told her story to her community for the first time at the march.

Wiping away tears, she said: "To a survivor listening right now, I want to say you are not dirty, you are not broken beyond repair. You are not to blame and you are not alone."

This is part of the Global Women series from the BBC World Service, sharing untold and important stories from around the globe

articles.title: Fiona the hippo's tragic death prompts Cincinnati Zoo to install new safeguards at Hippo Cove
articles.summary: New safety protections have been introduced at Hippo Cove as the Cincinnati Zoo reopens following Fiona's death, with guests urged to secure belongings.
articles.body: The Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden officially reopened its Hippo Cove exhibit on Monday, introducing new safety measures just days after the death of Fiona, the zoo’s famous 9-year-old Nile hippopotamus. Fiona died on Thursday, Nov. 19, after swallowing a visitor’s knitted hat that was accidentally deflected into her enclosure. Zoo officials shut down the habitat "to give keepers space" following the incident, according to a Monday news release. While Hippo Cove already met "strict" industry guidelines, zoo leaders said additional safeguards were installed before welcoming guests back. "Even though the habitat already met strict standards set by the [Association of Zoos and Aquariums], we made some modifications to guard against something like this ever happening again," Cincinnati Zoo Director Dave Jenike said in a statement. BELOVED HIPPO FIONA DIES AT CINCINNATI ZOO AFTER SWALLOWING VISITOR'S HAT "We added a layer of netting above the viewing windows and, out of an abundance of caution, removed all ceiling fans in the area." As the exhibit reopens to the public, visitors will be able to once again see Fiona's 27-year-old mother Bibi, 23-year-old Tucker, and her 4-year-old brother Fritz. Zoo leadership confirmed the hippos are "behaving normally" amid the loss. "They have been getting extra care, attention, a few more pumpkins, and according to the Zoo’s director of animal care, are behaving normally," the news release noted. Despite the upgraded barriers, zoo officials stress that they still rely on guests to secure their personal belongings, take extra care near all animal habitats, and notify staff immediately "if they see something that shouldn’t be in a habitat." ZOO SHARES NECROPSY FINDINGS FOLLOWING FIONA THE HIPPO’S HEARTBREAKING DEATH "The Cincinnati Zoo has been accredited since 1978 and was last accredited in 2025 after an exhaustive inspection, a standard practice for Zoos seeking or renewing accreditation," Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) President Dan Ashe said in a statement. "Nothing was of concern for the hippo habitat in the inspection report. It seems like it was a freak event that couldn’t have been foreseen. Our hearts go out to all the professionals at the Cincinnati Zoo. I know they are [devastated] by this." Macy’s also announced via its Instagram story that it will honor Fiona during the upcoming 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, according to People magazine. "Fiona brought joy to millions, including so many in the Macy’s community in Cincinnati. This year, as Macy’s welcomes our own beloved Blue Hippo back to the Parade, we wanted to mark Fiona’s memory," the retailer said. "With the Cincinnati Zoo’s blessing, Macy’s has made a donation to the zoo in Fiona’s memory and Blue Hippo’s handlers will wear a purple Fiona patch during the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade." EXCLUSIVE: NIH FUNDED FOREIGN LABS WITH TROUBLING SAFETY LAPSES, INCLUDING DEADLY BAT VIRUS EXPERIMENT Fiona captured the hearts of people all over the country after surviving an early birth in January 2017. Born six weeks early at just 29 pounds, Fiona rapidly drew enthusiastic online followers. Her death occurred roughly a decade after another high-profile demise at the same zoo, when Harambe, a 17-year-old western lowland gorilla, was fatally shot by zoo staff in May 2016 after a young boy climbed into his enclosure.
