articles.title: Ukraine’s drone strike on Russian warship in Libya risks ‘serious escalation,’ former official warns
articles.summary: Morgan Murphy warned the Ukrainian sea drone strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in Benghazi risks a serious escalation of the nearly five-year war.
articles.body: The Ukrainian sea drone strike that capsized and sank a Russian warship in Libya on Sunday risks a "serious escalation" of the nearly five-year war, a former U.S. national security adviser warned Monday, calling the operation a "giant tantrum" by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Morgan Murphy, a former press secretary to the secretary of defense, also told Fox News Digital that the nighttime attack on the Russian corvette Mercury in the Libyan port city of Benghazi could further strain relations between Zelenskyy and President Donald Trump, while echoing frustrations that he said also plagued former President Joe Biden's administration. "The strike on the Russian corvette Mercury in North Africa — in Libya specifically — is a serious escalation of the war in Ukraine," Murphy claimed. "Calling the Benghazi strike a giant tantrum could be one interpretation of it, and it's not unusual behavior for him," Murphy said of Zelenskyy. RUSSIAN WARSHIP SINKS OFF LIBYA AS SUSPECTED UKRAINIAN STRIKES TAKE WAR BEYOND BLACK SEA Murphy also argued that Zelenskyy's willingness to pursue military objectives that complicate Washington's diplomatic priorities has frustrated previous administrations. "This is why I think the Biden administration was frustrated with Zelenskyy, and why the Trump administration has been frustrated with Zelenskyy: he's acting like an independent player and not an ally," Murphy said. Biden had reportedly lost his temper during a June 2022 phone call after Zelenskyy requested additional military assistance shortly after the White House announced a $1 billion aid package for Ukraine. In his recently released memoir, Biden also revealed private frustrations with Zelenskyy, describing the Ukrainian leader as moody, stubborn and less grateful than expected. UKRAINE POUNDS BLACK SEA FLEET’S ‘LAST MAJOR STRONGHOLD’ WHILE PUTIN FLEXES NAVAL POWER IN PACIFIC Murphy went on to suggest the Benghazi drone strike could also complicate Trump's efforts to broker an end to the war, particularly after the president met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping at a historic summit without Zelenskyy. "The President just had a successful meeting with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping, and he met them without Zelenskyy present, as is the right of the President of the United States to meet with whom he likes when he pleases," Murphy said. "Zelenskyy was clearly upset about that, and this attack is him showing the President of the United States that he's still very relevant." The operation, coordinated by Ukraine's SBU intelligence agency and armed forces, targeted the Russian vessel in port, raising questions about where the drones originated and whether the conflict could spread further beyond Ukraine's borders. Zelenskyy praised the strike Monday in a post on X, calling it "An exemplary Ukrainian operation in response to Russia's war." Murphy argued that the Ukrainian leader is increasingly under pressure to demonstrate Kyiv can still deliver significant military victories as Trump pursues a diplomatic resolution. "What he's looking for here is, I believe, a victory, because Ukraine has found more aid and sympathy on the world stage when it's winning," Murphy said. Ukraine initially drew widespread international support after resisting Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, defying expectations that Moscow would quickly overwhelm Kyiv. "Ukraine performed much better against an enemy five times its size, and human nature loves an underdog." "There was a deep outpouring of sympathy — and more importantly, support — for Ukraine after that initial flop of a Russian invasion," Murphy said. UKRAINE'S ATTACKS ON RUSSIA ARE PUSHING PUTIN CLOSER TO NEGOTIATING TABLE, TRUMP NATO AMBASSADOR SAYS But as the conflict has dragged on, Murphy argued, Ukraine has struggled to sustain the enthusiasm that followed Russia's initial setbacks, with the fighting descending into what he described as a "stalemate and a war of attrition." "Zelenskyy is having a harder time building support," he said of the current state of play. "As he saw the President meet with Russia and meet with Xi Jinping in China, he needed a victory, and he needed a dramatic attack — so an asymmetric attack was on the board." The Benghazi strike also underscores Ukraine's expanding ability to target Russian military assets thousands of miles from its territory, although questions remain about how the operation was carried out. "Ukraine has taken credit for it, but they've been coy about where it was launched from," Murphy said. "There's some speculation that it was launched from within Libya. Others say that it came from a mothership, which is totally plausible — that they took an innocuous-looking cargo ship and launched these drones out of it." Murphy said the operation reflects a broader transformation in modern warfare, with military planners still grappling with the implications of increasingly sophisticated drone attacks. "What we are watching unfold in real time is a total shift in the nature of warfare. It's really unheralded," he said. UKRAINE’S DRONE REVOLUTION SHOWS RUSSIA IS DANGEROUSLY UNPREPARED. BUT, SO IS AMERICA "It will take time — planners' time and nations' time — to understand how to react to this kind of aggression." Beyond the military implications, Murphy warned that the strike could undermine diplomatic efforts in Washington to negotiate an end to the conflict. "There is a very concerted group of diplomats and thought leaders in D.C. who want to see a diplomatic end to this conflict sooner rather than later," Murphy said. "They see that as being in the best interest of the United States and the world, but most importantly, they see it in the best interest of the Ukrainian people." Murphy said those pushing for a negotiated settlement would likely view the reported strike in Libya as a setback to Trump's peace efforts. articles.title: Analysis: Can Andy Burnham turn volume down on UK rejoining EU debate?
articles.summary: The BBC's Chris Mason analyses what the EU conversation means for Labour and the PM.
articles.body:
When the prime minister told MPs "there will be no banging on about Europe" from him, my mind flashed back 20 years.

It is 2006 and a fresh faced David Cameron had just taken over as the Conservative leader , promising, yes you guessed it, to stop "banging on" about Europe.

And we all know how that turned out: a decade later as prime minister, he held and lost a referendum on whether the UK should stay in the European Union, as he advocated, or leave.

Andy Burnham's address to the Commons, after Friday's EU-UK Summit in Brussels, felt like an attempt by a man who chose to turn the Europe conversation up to full blast this autumn, to try to turn the volume back down again.

All of this prompts two big questions: whether he will be able to do that and what, in the end, Labour promises at the next general election.

Asked if that could include seeking a mandate for another in/out referendum at that election, he didn't rule that out.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't," he said.

But he very carefully left his options open: "There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination."

So he might offer a referendum. Or he might not.

My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham

He also suggested the frequency of his public utterances on the subject may be limited, insisting there would be no "running commentary," offering instead what he called "a calm, constructive and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain's interest in the long term."

Plus, he said Europe could change in the coming years. A nod, without naming her, that Marine Le Pen could become president of France, for instance. How might that shift the debate?

Burnham's willingness to repeatedly talk about the European question in the last few months has, inevitably, spawned quite the reaction.

A campaign group, Stay Out, has got itself up and running to argue exactly that.

And the European Movement is helping launch a rival outfit called, again, you guessed it, Get In.

It is a reminder that that the EU question has a knack of getting under the skin of British politics, often to the exclusion of other things, sometimes to the exclusion of seemingly everything.

Can the prime minister successfully manage the volume switch so the topic is background hubbub in 2027, rather than a deafening din?

Meanwhile, what does the European Union itself make of all of this? EU sources see Andy Burnham's desire to "brainstorm" with them what the future relationship might look like as "normal diplomacy" as one figure put it, adding: "I don't think there are many options. And they are clear. The status quo. The customs union. The single market. And full membership."

They mirror his expectation that "brainstorming" won't involve additional meetings, let alone a structured set of bespoke talks arriving at a conclusion. "We don't need a template. It will be part of the regular discussion," is how it was put to me.

On Thursday, the government will publish its European Partnerships Bill, the legislation needed to enact, at the UK end, the agreements reached at the summit. Also later this week, the legal text of those agreements is due to be published – the small print of which will be pored over.

How much might the UK have to compensate the EU for, for instance, if a future government were to decide to reverse the changes that have just been signed up to? Within the deal it is expected that were Britain to change its mind on the food export part of the deal in the next 10 years, Brussels would charge London for the reinstallation of the checkpoints that will soon no longer be needed.

Then, there are the ongoing negotiations between the two sides about unresolved areas of potential cooperation. The EU has made much of its desire to secure a deal on university tuition fees in the next six months, with the hope that EU students will pay no more at UK universities than British students do. The deal would be reciprocal for UK students studying elsewhere in Europe. Both sides think an agreement is within reach. Senior figures in Whitehall are also encouraged by the EU's willingness to include the UK in its 'Made in Europe' plan to protect European industry from China. Then there is the EU's common electricity market.

But even if all these things are agreed – and they will all provoke debate here about whether or not they are good ideas – Andy Burnham has publicly said incremental changes only take the UK so far.

It is clear he has an appetite and an interest in going further. The question, ultimately, is how much further?

articles.title: Four illegal immigrants among six arrested in Florida slaughterhouse torture case, AG says
articles.summary: Six workers at Ali Meat International, an Orlando halal slaughterhouse, face animal cruelty charges as four are held on ICE detainers, officials say.
articles.body: Customers could buy an animal and slaughter it themselves at a public event in Orlando, where video of what happened next led to six arrests and drew a rebuke from Florida’s attorney general, who called it "pure evil." Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Monday that six workers at Ali Meat International, a halal slaughterhouse, face charges in the case. In a post on X, he singled out four workers he said were in the country illegally. "Florida will not tolerate the abuse and torture of defenseless animals," Uthmeier wrote. "Four are illegal aliens who never should have been here, and they will be punished and sent back to where they came from." ICE-LED FLORIDA OPERATION NETS 500 — INCLUDING ILLEGAL ALIENS ACCUSED OF MURDER, CHILD ABUSE, CARTEL TIES U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement placed detainers on those four workers, according to Uthmeier’s office. At Monday’s press conference, Uthmeier said the state would prosecute them before any deportations. State agricultural agents arrested the six workers Friday while serving a warrant at the business. Among them was manager Nadeem Shakeel, 44, who faces up to 105 years in prison if convicted as charged, according to the attorney general’s office. WOMAN PLEADS GUILTY TO PAYING FOR SEXUAL TORTURE VIDEOS INVOLVING MONKEYS FOR ONLINE GROUP: 'SICK PERSON' U.S. Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins said federal food safety investigators reviewed video from the facility and found violations of federal humane slaughter law. She said USDA immediately revoked the facility’s permission to slaughter livestock without federal inspectors present. Rollins said USDA’s Office of Inspector General joined Florida authorities in Friday’s operation and that she was in Orlando to thank investigators. WARNING: GRAPHIC DETAILS "Animal cruelty is unacceptable," Rollins wrote. "We will hold those responsible accountable." The state opened its investigation in August 2025 after a person who saw the June event advertised on social media turned over 19 videos. In one recording, investigators say, a worker put a knife in the hand of a boy believed to be 12 or 13, then held his wrist to make him cut a sheep’s throat. "Subjecting children firsthand to this horrific behavior is unthinkable," Uthmeier said at the press conference. CALIFORNIA TEEN FACES PRISON AFTER VIRAL VIDEO SHOWS HIM SQUARING UP, REPEATEDLY KICKING SEA LION IN THE FACE Investigators said the videos showed workers carrying 16 lambs upside down by their legs, cutting their throats and tossing them into a pile. An employee walked over the lambs while several were still moving, according to Uthmeier’s office. Investigators also said cattle were repeatedly shocked with electric prods, including in the mouth and face, and that one customer made at least 15 cuts as an animal struggled to breathe. 69 LIVE ANIMALS FOUND STUFFED IN PILLOWCASES IN HIDDEN CAR COMPARTMENT AFTER BORDER ARREST: FEDS Assistant Statewide Prosecutor Lauryn Day said complaints about the business dated back to 2021. During Friday’s search, she said, investigators found live animals standing in mud and feces and storage areas littered with dirty socks and trash. The animals were placed in temporary care while the state works with the U.S. Department of Agriculture to arrange their transfer. "Religious beliefs do not provide a license to disregard animal welfare laws or subject animals to unnecessary suffering," Day said. Florida Agriculture Commissioner Wilton Simpson said his department was investigating other animal cruelty cases and urged anyone who knows about similar practices to come forward. "We’re not going to tolerate animal cruelty here in the state of Florida," he said. Shakeel told investigators he organized the event, oversaw staff and customers and handled the money, according to Uthmeier’s office. Agents said they found a stolen rifle in the office that Shakeel acknowledged was his. He faces a firearm theft charge in addition to animal cruelty, cattle abuse and conspiracy charges. Another worker, Gelacio Santiz, told investigators he began slaughtering animals while they were still conscious, the office said. The attorney general’s office identified the four workers with ICE detainers. Gelacio Santiz, 36, and Lorenzo Santis Diaz, 26, are from Mexico. Muhammad Irfan Khan, 44, is from Pakistan, and Jean Deolis, 57, is from Haiti. VIDEO SHOWS FLORIDA FOOD TRUCK WORKERS FLEEING FROM ICE DURING TALLAHASSEE IMMIGRATION RAID Belal Khaled Dohast, 45, was also arrested and faces animal cruelty and conspiracy charges. All six were being held at the Orange County Jail as of Monday’s announcement. Day said each had made an initial court appearance and that their bond conditions bar them from contacting one another, having contact with animals or returning to the business. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Uthmeier said the slaughterhouse was no longer operating as of Monday and that the state was considering civil action. His office said the criminal investigation remains open and more charges are expected.

articles.title: $98 million civil judgment awarded in Ohio rape that could not be prosecuted
articles.summary: An Ohio woman who survived a brutal rape that went unsolved for decades was awarded a $98 million civil judgment against her attacker, a doctor who admitted to the assault but could not be prosecuted for it because the statute of limitations had expired.
articles.body: An Ohio woman who survived a brutal rape that went unsolved for decades was awarded a $98 million civil judgment against her attacker, a doctor who admitted to the assault but could not be prosecuted for it because the statute of limitations had expired. Hamilton County Court of Common Pleas Judge Christopher McDowell awarded $48.2 million in compensatory damages and $50 million in punitive damages on Thursday to Dana Beatty in connection with the 1989 rape at her Cincinnati home, documents filed Friday show. McDowell described the punitive damages — which are meant to address especially egregious conduct — as “warranted and constitutionally proportionate” because the conduct of Frederick Tanzer was “intentional, violent, prolonged, and extraordinarily reprehensible.” Although Tanzer, 67, could not be prosecuted for the rape, he pleaded guilty to lying to federal authorities about it and was sentenced in January to 15 years in prison. In an interview with “Dateline” earlier this year, Tanzer admitted to the rape and said he was “working on the why.” Beatty filed the complaint against Tanzer in January 2025, alleging battery and intentional infliction of emotional distress. Tanzer did not respond to the complaint, McDowell wrote, nor did he appear at a Nov. 17 hearing on the matter. He did not have an attorney in the proceedings, according to McDowell. In an interview Monday, Beatty said she was shocked by the massive judgment but grateful to McDowell for his understanding of the “complex, lifelong ramifications the crime had on my life and my family’s.” The size of the judgment, she said, demonstrated that understanding. “Unless you have been through a crime of this magnitude, it’s hard to comprehend the lifelong and massive repercussions that the victim and her family have to live with the rest of their lives,” she said. Beatty said she would be pleasantly surprised if she were to recover any of the damages. Beatty was assaulted for hours on Aug. 1, 1989, by a masked man armed with a knife and wearing a black lycra bodysuit. He wrapped her face in tape, lashed to her to a bed and left an ominous note, telling Beatty — who at the time worked for IBM — “no police, or I’ll be back, Miss IBM,” authorities have said. The case remained cold until 2023, when DNA recovered from Beatty’s dress was matched to Tanzer. At the time of the attack, Tanzer was married to Beatty’s best friend. Tanzer could not be prosecuted for the rape since Ohio’s statute of limitations was just six years in 1989. But in 2024, local and federal authorities began pursuing what one investigator described as a last-ditch effort to hold Tanzer accountable: They planned to catch him in a lie about his role in the crime. When investigators questioned Tanzer about the assault, he told them that he hadn’t had sex with Beatty or gone to her apartment on Aug. 1, 1989. He was arrested on suspicion of making false statements to a federal agent, a charge he pleaded guilty to in September 2025. Ohio’s statute of limitations for rape is now 25 years, and it can be extended an additional five years if a DNA match is made with a possible suspect. But Beatty’s case highlights the often-uneven manner in which time limits are applied to some of the most serious sexual assault cases in the United States. An NBC News analysis from all 50 states and Washington D.C. found that time limits for adult victims differ dramatically among the more than 30 states that have them. While nearly a dozen states eliminate statutes of limitations if DNA evidence comes into play, 14 either offer limited DNA extensions of five years or less or no extension at all. In Montana, the statute of limitations for aggravated sexual intercourse without consent — that state’s most serious rape charge — is five years, with a one-year DNA extension. In New Hampshire, the time limit is six years, with no DNA extension. Beatty said Monday that she hopes to use the civil judgment as momentum to help other victims change statute of limitations laws.

articles.title: Trump’s direct call, Vance’s 72-hour push: How White House got Nvidia to reinstate Huang as CEO
articles.summary: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer, reversing its decision to remove him just 11 days earlier following revelations about
articles.body: Nvidia has reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive officer, reversing its decision to remove him just 11 days earlier following revelations about his reported extramarital relationships, including one involving a woman suspected by US officials of having links to Chinese intelligence. The announcement triggered a sharp rally in the company's shares, adding $952 billion to its market value in a single trading session.The reinstatement followed an extraordinary intervention by US president Donald Trump, who mobilised senior administration officials, including vice president JD Vance, to persuade Nvidia's board to bring Huang back. Trump personally contacted board members to vouch for the executive, whom he considers critical to America's artificial intelligence ambitions and its economic competition with China.According to people familiar with the matter cited by CNN, Trump had been concerned about the impact of Huang's departure on the stock market and the broader US economy. He ultimately concluded that restoring the Nvidia chief was necessary to stabilise investor confidence and prevent the country from losing a key figure in the global AI race.The decision marked a reversal after the company’s board had publicly described his conduct as “inconsistent with the company’s code of conduct, standards and cultural norms”.Vance led White House pressure campaignTrump tasked Vance with working directly with Huang and Nvidia’s board to facilitate the reinstatement. The vice-president became the administration’s principal emissary, using his connections in Silicon Valley to persuade board members to reconsider their position.The Associated Press reported that Vance stepped up his involvement over the weekend to make Trump’s case to the board.The person familiar with the matter told AP that the White House believed Vance, who had worked in Silicon Valley before entering politics, had the stature to help board members overcome their reservations about bringing Huang back.CNN reported that Vance coordinated directly with Huang over 72 hours, assuring the board that the government had found no evidence that the CEO had committed anything illegal or threatened national security.Commerce secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury secretary Scott Bessent were also involved in the effort, according to CNN. Their involvement came amid reported disagreements within the administration over the handling of Nvidia chip sales to China.Trump also contacted Nvidia’s board directly to vouch for Huang, whom he considers an important adviser on AI policy and a key figure in maintaining America's technological advantage over Beijing.According to news agency Reuters, US attorney general Todd Blanche and director of national intelligence Jay Clayton also played roles in determining Huang was not a security risk to the US and did not see any evidence that he did anything illegal or untoward related to US national security.Speaking to CNBC on Monday, Trump acknowledged his role in the decision. “I believe my intervention was very important,” he said.Trump added that he had spoken to Huang on Sunday and that the executive had promised to work harder following his return.“The board decided to do what we wanted them to do,” Trump said.“I’ve been speaking to the board directly and indirectly, and I felt very strongly about it,” he added.The president also said, “I think we have one of our great stars back in play.”Scandal and China concernsThe intervention followed concerns about Huang’s reported extramarital relationships, including one involving Alice Huang, a woman US officials suspected could have links to Chinese intelligence. Another relationship reportedly involved a direct subordinate.Alice Huang was an executive at Megaspeed, a company that purchased Nvidia chips, which US officials feared could subsequently have reached China. The precise nature of her alleged intelligence connections remains unclear.Nvidia’s board said it would complete its investigation into the national security concerns. Meanwhile, the Commerce Department is adding Megaspeed to the US Entity List, restricting its access to US exports, according to a notice scheduled for publication in the Federal Register.The financial implications of Huang’s return were immediate. Nvidia shares surged more than 30%, recording their third-best trading day on record and adding $952 billion to the company's market value. The Nasdaq Composite rose 6.51%.Forbes estimated Huang’s fortune at approximately $143 billion, a single-day increase of $33 billion.Huang is scheduled to testify before the Senate Banking Committee next Thursday, where questions about his conduct, Nvidia’s China strategy and the administration’s intervention are expected to remain under scrutiny.You use AI every day. articles.title: Germany turned an abandoned steel factory into a 180-hectare public park; its old gasometer became a diving centre and former ore bunkers now serve as climbing gardens
articles.summary: An abandoned steelworks in Duisburg, Germany, might seem an unlikely place to spend a day walking, cycling or swimming.
articles.body: An abandoned steelworks in Duisburg, Germany, might seem an unlikely place to spend a day walking, cycling or swimming. Yet the vast industrial site has found a second life as a public park, where remnants of its manufacturing past sit alongside gardens, waterways and outdoor recreation facilities. Spread across 180 hectares, Landschaftspark Duisburg-Nord has turned structures once used for iron production into spaces for leisure and adventure. An old gasometer now houses a diving facility, former ore bunkers have become climbing areas, and visitors can climb a disused blast furnace for views across the surrounding landscape. The transformation began in the 1990s, giving the former industrial complex a new purpose without erasing its history.Germany's abandoned steel factory becomes a 180-hectare public parkLandschaftspark Duisburg-Nord occupies the grounds of a former ironworks in Duisburg, in Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia region. Rather than clearing the industrial structures after production ended, the redevelopment retained much of the existing complex and incorporated it into a large recreational landscape.The park opened in 1994 and brought together industrial architecture, natural spaces and facilities for public use. Its old buildings and machinery remain visible throughout the grounds, providing a record of the site's manufacturing history. Over time, the former steelworks developed into a destination that attracts around one million visitors annually. It has also received international recognition, including a place on The Guardian's list of the world's ten most beautiful urban oases.An old gasometer becomes a diving destinationOne of the most unusual features of the park is its diving centre, housed inside a former gasometer. A structure that once served an industrial purpose has been converted into a large underwater training and recreation facility, described by the park's operators as Europe's largest artificial diving centre. The facility gives diving enthusiasts an opportunity to practise in an enclosed environment rather than travelling to a natural lake or coastal location. Its setting is also a reminder of how the site's industrial infrastructure has been adapted for activities far removed from its original function.Former ore bunkers are now climbing gardensThe park's former ore storage bunkers have also taken on a different role. These imposing concrete structures, once used to store raw materials for iron production, now form an alpine-style climbing garden. Their existing walls and surfaces provide the setting for climbing routes, bringing an outdoor sporting activity into the heart of the old industrial complex.Elsewhere, a former casting house has been adapted to accommodate a high ropes course. Visitors can take on elevated challenges within a building that was once part of the steelmaking process. The park also has a large tube slide running through two ore bunkers, making the industrial structures part of a play area for younger visitors.Blast furnaces offer views across the siteSome of the park's most recognisable structures have been retained as viewing points. A disused blast furnace has been fitted with a viewing platform, allowing visitors to climb up and look across the grounds and surrounding parts of Duisburg.Blast Furnace 5 is among the attractions visitors can explore. The elevated viewpoints provide a different perspective on the scale of the former ironworks, with its network of industrial buildings, open spaces and surviving structures visible from above.The grounds themselves are open to people who prefer a slower visit. Gardens, meadows and water features have been incorporated into the landscape, with walking and cycling routes connecting different sections of the park. Visitors can bring their own bicycles or use the available hire facilities. An e-bike charging station is also provided.Guided tours offer another way to understand the site. These visits explain the history of the ironworks and the industrial processes once carried out there, giving context to the buildings that now accommodate recreational activities.A park designed for families and evening visitorsLandschaftspark Duisburg-Nord is not limited to climbing and diving. Children and families have access to play areas, a children's farm and other attractions spread across the former factory grounds. The combination of open spaces and repurposed industrial structures means that different age groups can explore the site in their own way.After dark, the park takes on a different appearance. British artist Jonathan Park created a lighting installation that illuminates the old ironworks with changing colours. The evening display highlights the outlines of the industrial buildings and machinery, turning the structures into a prominent feature of the night-time landscape.For first-time visitors, the park's visitor centre is a useful starting point. Maps and information about the grounds, activities and guided tours are available there, helping people plan their route through the extensive site.Preserving industrial history through reuseLandschaftspark Duisburg-Nord demonstrates an approach to redevelopment in which former industrial buildings are retained and given new uses instead of being removed altogether. The gasometer, ore bunkers, casting house and blast furnace continue to define the character of the grounds, even though their functions have changed.The site is operated by Duisburg Kontor Hallenmanagement GmbH. More than three decades after opening as a public park in 1994, it remains a place where Duisburg's industrial past and present-day recreational life occupy the same landscape.You use AI every day.
